title: Point-Slope Form: Why the Subtractions Matter

scenes.title: Given one point and a slope — what equation fits?
body: We need every point on the line to keep the same rate from (-4, 7).
scenes.narration: Suppose a line has slope negative two and passes through negative four comma seven. How can we write its equation without first hunting for the y-intercept? Here is the idea: slope compares the change from one point to another. If negative four comma seven is our known point, then every other point x comma y on the line must change from it at the same rate, negative two. Point-slope form is built directly from that idea.

scenes.title: Where point-slope form comes from
body: Slope = change in y ÷ change in x.
The known point supplies the starting coordinates.
scenes.narration: Start with what slope means: change in y divided by change in x. Using a known point x one comma y one, the vertical change is y minus y one, and the horizontal change is x minus x one. Multiply both sides by x minus x one, and you get y minus y one equals m times x minus x one. Notice why the formula uses subtraction: it is measuring change from the known point, not storing random signs to memorize.

scenes.title: This is where signs cause mistakes
body: Use the coordinates as signed values first.
scenes.narration: Now substitute the slope negative two and the point negative four comma seven. Write y minus seven equals negative two times x minus negative four. This is where students often mix things up: they copy the coordinate sign directly and write x minus four. But the formula already contains subtraction. Since x one is negative four, x minus negative four becomes x plus four. Keeping the signed coordinate inside parentheses first prevents that mistake.

scenes.title: Why this equation must pass through the point
body: At x = -4, the horizontal change is 0.
So the vertical change must also be 0.
scenes.narration: Why does this form guarantee the line passes through the given point? Put x equals negative four into the equation. The quantity x plus four becomes zero. So the right side is zero, which forces y minus seven to equal zero, giving y equals seven. The known point is built into the equation automatically. The slope controls how y changes once you move away from that point.

scenes.title: Quick check: convert and verify the slope
body: Expand only after the point-slope equation is correct.
Slope stays -2; the line still passes through (-4, 7).
scenes.narration: As a quick check, expand: y minus seven equals negative two x minus eight, so y equals negative two x minus one. The slope is still negative two, and substituting x equals negative four gives y equals eight minus one, which is seven. So everything matches. The big idea is that point-slope form describes change from a known point: subtract the point's coordinates, keep their signs intact, and let the slope connect the two changes.
